ig_caption:
Why does one win give you a handful of points, while one loss takes a lot more? It all depends on who you played.

Before every rated game, the site makes a guess: the player with the higher rating should score more. If you do better than that guess, you gain points. If you do worse, you lose them.

So beating a stronger player gives more points, and losing to a weaker one costs more. Even a draw against someone stronger can push your rating up. Against an equal, a win and a loss move it by about the same amount.

The simple lesson: judge your progress by the shape of your graph over a month, not by one game.

slides.title: +5 for a win, −12 for a loss?
slides.sub: HOW RATING POINTS ARE WORKED OUT

slides.title: The site makes a guess
slides.body: Before every rated game, the site expects the player with the higher rating to score more. Do better than its guess and you gain points. Do worse and you lose them.
slides.note: The bigger the gap between you, the more one-sided the guess.

slides.title: Who you play matters
slides.body: Beat someone rated well above you and you gain a lot. Lose to someone well below you and you drop a lot. Against an equal, a win and a loss are about the same size.
slides.note: A small win against a weaker player is still a job well done.

slides.title: Draws count too
slides.body: A draw is half a win. Draw with someone stronger and you did better than the guess, so your rating goes up. Draw with someone weaker and it can go down.
slides.note: Holding a draw against a stronger player is worth being proud of.

slides.title: Judge the line, not the game
slides.body: One game tells you very little. Look at the shape of your graph over a month: is it slowly rising, flat or falling? That is your real progress.
slides.note: One upset loss is a dip, not a trend.

slides.title: Every plus and every minus
slides.sub: Your whole rating history, on one print.
